title: Rethinking Memorization Mitigation inDiffusion Models: Reinforcing Text Conditioning

paper.title: Rethinking Memorization Mitigation in Diffusion Models: Reinforcing Text Conditioning
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-to-image diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in image synthesis, yet can exhibit memorization by closely reproducing individual training examples. Effective mitigation must preserve useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions. We introduce a training-free method that redistributes cross-attention with Gaussian smoothing before reinforcing content-token contributions and attenuating padding contributions, without additional denoiser evaluations. With this intervention, stronger content conditioning can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity. A local analysis identifies when reinforcement preserves shared value information while redistribution reduces localized attention mass. On Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus both prompt alignment and image preference. A configuration selected on Stable Diffusion reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning. These findings support jointly controlling conditioning allocation and strength to generate prompt-consistent alternatives.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models enable high-quality image synthesis from natural-language descriptions ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Yet these models can exhibit memorization : certain prompts elicit close reproductions of individual training images ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Somepalli et al., 2023b ; Webster, 2023 ) . Such reproduction can preserve a training image’s distinctive composition and visual details, beyond the semantic resemblance expected from depicting the same subject. Mitigating this behavior requires more than moving the generated image away from a training reference: the model must still produce a useful alternative that follows the prompt. A prompt generally permits many valid depictions, and its objects, attributes, and context provide information for constructing them. Figure 1 illustrates this goal: the film context in the Emma Watson/Belle prompt supports an alternative depiction of the subject. Several inference-time approaches mitigate memorization by weakening or avoiding conditional responses associated with reproduction. Prompt-embedding adjustment reduces the magnitude of text-conditional guidance ( Wen et al., 2024 ) , while initial-noise adjustment seeks starting points with weaker conditional responses and earlier escape from memorization basins ( Han et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches postpone or reverse guidance ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , or reduce attention to prompt words ( Ren et al., 2024 ) . We instead make content reinforcement an active part of mitigation: strengthening useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions. We find that content reinforcement can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity. This improvement occurs when content gain is increased with redistribution and padding attenuation held fixed, showing that reinforcement can support useful conditioning during mitigation. We implement this approach as a training-free cross-attention intervention that combines content amplification with Gaussian redistribution and selective padding attenuation. Early smoothing changes the allocation of attention across token positions; amplification then strengthens the redistributed content contributions. The intervention retains the original prompt and frozen model and requires no additional denoiser evaluations. Figure 1: Reinforce a redistributed conditioning pattern. (a) An illustrative attention row shows Gaussian redistribution followed by content reinforcement and padding attenuation, on a shared scale. (b) Recorded outputs illustrate an alternative depiction that retains the prompt context. Redistribution improves the suppression–quality balance of this reinforcement strategy. At fixed token gains in our main configuration, Gaussian redistribution recovers prompt alignment and image preference over reweighting alone while retaining most of the suppression. A local analysis complements these generation-level results: under value-coherence conditions, an admissible gain preserves shared feature information while reducing the attention component’s mass on its original token set. Together, these results explain how controlling attention allocation supports reinforcement during mitigation. On two Stable Diffusion benchmarks, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus prompt alignment and image preference. A direction–norm control shows that suppression persists after restoring guidance magnitude. Our configuration selected on Stable Diffusion also transfers to DeepFloyd IF without IF-specific tuning. These findings support content reinforcement as a means of generating useful alternatives while mitigating reproduction.

sections.heading: Memorization in diffusion models.
sections.text: Training-image extraction and replication studies show that diffusion models can reproduce individual training examples ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ) . Data duplication and image–caption associations influence this behavior ( Somepalli et al., 2023b ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Mechanistic analyses locate memorization-related neurons in cross-attention layers ( Hintersdorf et al., 2024 ) , while geometric analyses explain memorization through the relationship between learned and data manifolds ( Ross et al., 2025 ) . Reproduction also takes different forms: Webster (2023) documents both image and template reproduction, and Bright Ending ( Chen et al., 2025 ) examines local memorization in which only part of an image is copied. These perspectives provide complementary accounts of what is reproduced and how memorization is represented in the model.

sections.heading: Inference-time mitigation.
sections.text: Existing methods intervene at different points in generation. Random prompt perturbations disrupt the conditioning associated with reproduction ( Somepalli et al., 2023b ) , while gradient-based prompt adjustment optimizes text embeddings to reduce the magnitude of text-conditional noise predictions ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . Guidance-based methods delay or reverse classifier-free guidance to escape memorization basins ( Jain et al., 2025 ) ; Anti-Memorization Guidance combines guidance terms targeting image duplication, caption duplication, and prompt specificity ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . Initial-noise adjustment searches for starting points that permit earlier escape from memorization basins ( Han et al., 2025 ) . Bright Ending ( Chen et al., 2025 ) localizes copied regions using EOS-token attention at the final denoising step and uses the resulting spatial mask to focus detection and prompt optimization on those regions. For direct attention modification, Ren et al. (2024) combine summary-token masking with an increase in the start-of-sequence (SOS) token’s logit before softmax; the latter shifts attention toward SOS and reduces the attention weights assigned to prompt words. Our method instead redistributes attention across token positions before reinforcing content contributions, preserving the original prompt and initial noise without input optimization.

sections.heading: Attention control for semantic fidelity.
sections.text: Cross-attention control also supports the expression of prompt semantics. Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) reuses attention maps to preserve spatial layout during text-based image editing. Structured Diffusion ( Feng et al., 2023 ) incorporates linguistic structure into cross-attention guidance to improve compositional generation. SynGen ( Rassin et al., 2023 ) uses syntactic relations to align the attention maps of entities and their modifiers, improving attribute binding. Attend-and-Excite ( Chefer et al., 2023 ) addresses neglected subjects by smoothing their spatial attention maps and iteratively optimizing the latent to strengthen their activations. We share the goal of making generated images more faithfully reflect prompt content. Our intervention redistributes attention along token positions and directly amplifies the resulting content contributions, coupling this semantic objective with memorization mitigation rather than optimizing a subject-specific spatial attention objective.

sections.heading: 3 Reinforcing redistributed cross-attention
sections.text: We reinforce prompt content to support useful alternatives during mitigation, while controlling its allocation across token positions (Figure 1 ). We first redistribute attention, then reinforce content within the resulting pattern and selectively attenuate padding contributions. This order makes amplification act on a new mixture of token values. We formalize the operator, analyze reinforcement with localized dilution, and adapt it to DeepFloyd IF.

sections.heading: Redistribution: control the extent of mixing.
sections.text: A concentrated attention row repeatedly emphasizes a small part of the available value information. We first change this allocation by applying a normalized, truncated Gaussian kernel along token positions 1 , … , L − 1 1,\ldots,L-1 , using width σ \sigma and reflection padding. The start-token column is unchanged. Denote this operator by B k B_{k} . Gaussian weights provide a distance-dependent redistribution rule: nearby positions exchange more attention, and σ \sigma controls how widely each contribution spreads. This supplies a simple, tunable continuum from narrow mixing to broad redistribution without selecting individual subjects or optimizing a prompt-specific attention target. The positional kernel defines the extent of mixing; the value vectors determine what information that mixing retains. Local consistency of value information, formalized in Section 3.2 , governs this retention. Wider kernels dilute localized contributions more strongly but also mix across more varied values. We apply smoothing during an early denoising window to establish the redistributed conditioning pattern, then let B k B_{k} become the identity for the remaining steps. We use the first 5 of 50 steps for SD v1.4 and the first 10 for SD v2.0.

sections.heading: 3.3 Transfer to DeepFloyd IF
sections.text: IF uses T5 conditioning and attention over added text keys and image keys. We apply the same operator to Stage I’s text-key block. Because T5 has no CLIP start token, smoothing spans the entire text block; content positions precede EOS, and positions after EOS receive λ p \lambda_{p} . Image keys are unchanged, and Stage II uses its original attention. The transfer uses the SD-selected configuration without IF-specific strength tuning. This adaptation tests the design with a different text encoder and pixel-space denoising while retaining the same redistribution-and-reinforcement rule.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate whether redistribution and reinforcement can jointly reduce training-image similarity while retaining prompt-consistent generation. After benchmarking the suppression–quality trade-off, we test whether stronger content conditioning remains useful during mitigation (Figure 4 ), whether redistribution improves the trade-off at fixed token gains (Table 1 ), and whether the effect is explained by guidance magnitude alone (Table 2 ). We then examine the EOS suppression boundary, transfer to a different model family, and selective application with an existing detector.

sections.heading: Models and comparisons.
sections.text: The baseline benchmark uses 500 memorized prompts for SD v1.4 and 219 for SD v2.0 from prior work ( Webster, 2023 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) . We generate ten images per prompt with 50 steps and CFG scale 7, using DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) for v1.4 and Euler for v2.0. Baselines are random token addition (RTA; Somepalli et al., 2023b ), gradient-based prompt adjustment (GPA; Wen et al., 2024 ), cross-attention scaling (CS; Ren et al., 2024 ), opposite guidance with a dynamic transition point (DTP; Jain et al., 2025 ), and initial-noise adjustment (AIN; Han et al., 2025 ). Figure 2 includes every recorded operating point.

sections.heading: Design and mechanism studies.
sections.text: Controlled studies use SD v1.4 with the same DDIM schedule and CFG scale, producing 512 × 512 512\times 512 outputs. The EOS-boundary sweep covers 500 prompts with four images each; redistribution and guidance controls use a common subset of the same benchmark. Compared settings share initial random draws.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We assess training-image similarity with SSCD ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ) , prompt alignment with CLIP cosine similarity, and learned preference with ImageReward ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . In the controlled SD studies, each generated image is compared with its prompt’s available ground-truth references using the maximum SSCD, and scores are averaged over samples. Figure 2: Mitigation–quality trade-offs on (a) SD v1.4 and (b) SD v2.0. All recorded operating points are shown; lines connect settings within each method. Lower-right is preferable.

sections.heading: 4.2 Memorization–quality trade-offs
sections.text: Empirical Pareto-frontier performance. In Figure 2 , each of our four operating points lies on the empirical Pareto frontier in both the SSCD–CLIP and SSCD–ImageReward comparisons, on both models: no evaluated alternative improves one objective without worsening the other. Varying the width traverses this trade-off, with smaller widths favoring quality and larger widths favoring stronger suppression. For example, our method ( σ = 4 \sigma=4 ) and per-sample AIN (target 0.9) both report SSCD 0.2265 on SD v1.4; ours attains higher CLIP (0.2731 versus 0.2647) and ImageReward ( − 0.2374 -0.2374 versus − 0.3522 -0.3522 ). Against the attention-based CS baseline, our σ = 1 \sigma=1 setting attains lower SSCD and higher CLIP than every evaluated CS setting on both models. On SD v2.0, it also achieves higher ImageReward. Figure 3: Prompt-consistent alternatives. Comparison with GPA and CS for three prompts, with training references shown for context. Our method retains the green kitchen, fish-patterned blanket, and performance context in alternative compositions.

sections.heading: Prompt-consistent alternatives.
sections.text: Figure 3 compares how mitigation methods retain prompt content. For the performance prompt, GPA shows two people posing together, while CS shows a portrait of the subject. Our output depicts the subject performing with a handheld microphone, making the requested activity more explicit than in these baseline outputs while departing from the training reference’s guitar-playing composition. The kitchen and blanket examples further illustrate alternative depictions that retain the requested green interior and fish motif.

sections.heading: 4.3 Reinforcing redistributed content
sections.text: With Gaussian redistribution and padding suppression retained, λ w = 2 \lambda_{w}=2 yields higher CLIP than λ w = 1 \lambda_{w}=1 at comparable SSCD, as shown in Figure 4 . This improvement shows that stronger content conditioning can support prompt alignment without undoing the achieved suppression. Between these endpoints, SSCD responds non-monotonically: it first rises and then falls back to a comparable level at gain 2, while the wider sweep to 3 extends this decline. In the accompanying example, at λ w = 1 \lambda_{w}=1 the pillow is blue but the guitar is brown; at λ w = 2 \lambda_{w}=2 , the guitar itself is blue, matching the requested attribute. These observations support reinforcement as a means of expressing useful prompt information during mitigation, without uniformly strengthening reproduction of the training reference. sections.heading: 4.6 Preserving the first EOS token
sections.text: Content reinforcement and selective suppression play complementary roles. Reducing the padding gain lowers both SSCD and CLIP (Appendix D ), making the suppression boundary important for retaining useful conditioning. We therefore test whether attenuation should include the first EOS token. Figure 5 (a) varies its multiplier within our method. Preserving EOS yields favorable ImageReward–SSCD operating points across the measured sweep; extending attenuation to EOS reaches a lower similarity endpoint at a greater preference cost. At each fixed width, the additional suppression lowers both SSCD and ImageReward. The separate token-removal example in Figure 5 (b) illustrates the contextual information affected by this choice. sections.heading: 4.7 Transfer to DeepFloyd IF
sections.text: We test whether our SD-selected configuration transfers to T5-conditioned, pixel-space IF without target-specific tuning. Using template annotations ( Webster, 2023 ) , we evaluate 48 template-verbatim (TV) prompts across 11 shared-reference groups and three seeds (144 images per arm). As shown in Table 3 , our method reduces template matches from 38.89% to 20.14%. This reduction under the SD-selected settings shows that the intervention can suppress reproduction with a different text encoder and generation space. CLIP and ImageReward also decrease relative to the base model, so the transferred configuration retains a suppression benefit with a quality cost.

sections.heading: 4.8 Selective mitigation with an existing detector
sections.text: To limit intervention on ordinary prompts, we intervene at full strength ( σ = 4 \sigma=4 ) only on inputs flagged by the initial-step guidance detector of Wen et al. (2024) . At a calibrated 5% false-positive rate, mean SSCD on 500 memorized prompts falls from 0.5486 to 0.3475, versus 0.2078 when every prompt is treated. Average ImageReward changes by − 0.0065 -0.0065 over normal prompts and − 0.1291 -0.1291 within the flagged normal subset. Because unflagged inputs follow the original generation path, selective application preserves most normal generations while still reducing reproduction. Its weaker suppression than universal application reflects the memorization-prone prompts left untreated.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that stronger content conditioning within redistributed attention can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity, making reinforcement an active means of generating useful alternatives during mitigation. The local analysis identifies conditions under which reinforcement preserves shared value information while redistribution dilutes localized attention, and controlled comparisons show quality recovery from redistribution at fixed token gains. Our method attains empirical Pareto-frontier performance on two Stable Diffusion benchmarks. An SD-selected configuration also reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning. The resulting principle is to reinforce useful prompt content during mitigation, using redistribution to improve the balance between reproduction suppression and prompt-consistent generation.

sections.heading: Relation to the experimental design.
sections.text: The gain interval couples dilution to coherence. Wider smoothing can reduce retention on a localized set while increasing the transport-distance bound on feature distortion. Content reinforcement compensates for the latter within the admissible interval. After the early smoothing window, G = I G=I and the local interval disappears; subsequent reweighting acts on attention along the already modified trajectory. The analysis therefore motivates early redistribution coupled with reinforcement, while the reported schedule and gains are empirical design choices. The gain sweep and the row-mass and direction/norm controls assess the resulting allocation–strength trade-off through prompt alignment, image preference, and training-image similarity.

sections.heading: Computational checks.
sections.text: Numerical verification covers the finite-kernel inequalities, complete-row gain conditions, and transport bound, including equality-achieving profiles. Independent linear-programming checks confirm the sharp bound in Eq. ( 17 ). Verification scripts and detailed numerical results are included with the manuscript source. Four counterexamples delimit the analysis: useful information confined to the same isolated token can be attenuated; a uniform attention pattern can be amplified everywhere; reflection can change total row mass; and background inflow can outweigh a localized component’s dilution. These cases motivate the coherence, concentration, and full-row conditions used above.

sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation and reproducibility details
sections.text: The baseline benchmark was run on an A100 with PyTorch 1.13.0, torchvision 0.14.0, CUDA 11.7, and diffusers 0.26.3. The controlled SD and IF studies used an H100 80GB with PyTorch 2.5.1+cu121, diffusers 0.40.0, and transformers 5.12.1. ImageReward ran in a separate environment with transformers 4.30.2. The scorer for these studies uses OpenCLIP ViT-B-32 ( Cherti et al., 2023 ) with the laion2b_s34b_b79k checkpoint ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) ; SSCD uses sscd_disc_mixup ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ; Douze et al., 2021 ) ; preference evaluation uses ImageReward v1.0. Scores are computed against the original prompt. Comparisons are made within each environment and sampling protocol. We report paired percentile bootstrap CIs without multiplicity adjustment. The baseline benchmark and EOS sweep provide aggregate comparisons; prompt-level CIs are reported for the controlled SD studies. The controlled SD studies use DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) with 50 steps, CFG scale 7, and 512 × 512 512\times 512 outputs. Redistribution and guidance controls use a common 340-prompt subset of the 500-prompt benchmark, comprising 264 template-memorization (TM) and 76 verbatim-memorization (VM) prompts. The subset is stratified by memorization type, with identical captions and shared recorded ground-truth identifiers kept in the same partition. These controls use two seeds and four images per prompt and seed, with matched initial random draws across settings. Paired SD intervals first average samples and seeds within each prompt, then resample prompts with replacement 10,000 times. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.01723v1 [cs.CV] 01 Oct 2026 Rethinking Memorization Mitigation in Diffusion Models: Reinforcing Text Conditioning Hyungjun Joo Affiliation: Samsung Electronics Email: hyjun.joo@samsung.com Sehwan Kim Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: sehwankim@snu.ac.kr Hyeonggeun Han Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: hygnhan@snu.ac.kr Sangwoo Hong Affiliation: Konkuk University Email: swhong06@konkuk.ac.kr Jungwoo Lee Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: junglee@snu.ac.kr Abstract Text-to-image diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in image synthesis, yet can exhibit memorization by closely reproducing individual training examples. Effective mitigation must preserve useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions. We introduce a training-free method that redistributes cross-attention with Gaussian smoothing before reinforcing content-token contributions and attenuating padding contributions, without additional denoiser evaluations. With this intervention, stronger content conditioning can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity. A local analysis identifies when reinforcement preserves shared value information while redistribution reduces localized attention mass. On Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus both prompt alignment and image preference. A configuration selected on Stable Diffusion reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning. These findings support jointly controlling conditioning allocation and strength to generate prompt-consistent alternatives. 1 Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models enable high-quality image synthesis from natural-language descriptions ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Yet these models can exhibit memorization : certain prompts elicit close reproductions of individual training images ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Somepalli et al., 2023b ; Webster, 2023 ) . Such reproduction can preserve a training image’s distinctive composition and visual details, beyond the semantic resemblance expected from depicting the same subject. Mitigating this behavior requires more than moving the generated image away from a training reference: the model must still produce a useful alternative that follows the prompt. A prompt generally permits many valid depictions, and its objects, attributes, and context provide information for constructing them. Figure 1 illustrates this goal: the film context in the Emma Watson/Belle prompt supports an alternative depiction of the subject. Several inference-time approaches mitigate memorization by weakening or avoiding conditional responses associated with reproduction. Prompt-embedding adjustment reduces the magnitude of text-conditional guidance ( Wen et al., 2024 ) , while initial-noise adjustment seeks starting points with weaker conditional responses and earlier escape from memorization basins ( Han et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches postpone or reverse guidance ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , or reduce attention to prompt words ( Ren et al., 2024 ) . We instead make content reinforcement an active part of mitigation: strengthening useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions. We find that content reinforcement can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity. This improvement occurs when content gain is increased with redistribution and padding attenuation held fixed, showing that reinforcement can support useful conditioning during mitigation. We implement this approach as a training-free cross-attention intervention that combines content amplification with Gaussian redistribution and selective padding attenuation. Early smoothing changes the allocation of attention across token positions; amplification then strengthens the redistributed content contributions. The intervention retains the original prompt and frozen model and requires no additional denoiser evaluations. Figure 1: Reinforce a redistributed conditioning pattern. (a) An illustrative attention row shows Gaussian redistribution followed by content reinforcement and padding attenuation, on a shared scale. (b) Recorded outputs illustrate an alternative depiction that retains the prompt context. Redistribution improves the suppression–quality balance of this reinforcement strategy. At fixed token gains in our main configuration, Gaussian redistribution recovers prompt alignment and image preference over reweighting alone while retaining most of the suppression. A local analysis complements these generation-level results: under value-coherence conditions, an admissible gain preserves shared feature information while reducing the attention component’s mass on its original token set. Together, these results explain how controlling attention allocation supports reinforcement during mitigation. On two Stable Diffusion benchmarks, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus prompt alignment and image preference. A direction–norm control shows that suppression persists after restoring guidance magnitude. Our configuration selected on Stable Diffusion also transfers to DeepFloyd IF without IF-specific tuning. These findings support content reinforcement as a means of generating useful alternatives while mitigating reproduction. 2 Related work Memorization in diffusion models. Training-image extraction and replication studies show that diffusion models can reproduce individual training examples ( Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ) . Data duplication and image–caption associations influence this behavior ( Somepalli et al., 2023b ; Somepalli et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Mechanistic analyses locate memorization-related neurons in cross-attention layers ( Hintersdorf et al., 2024 ) , while geometric analyses explain memorization through the relationship between learned and data manifolds ( Ross et al., 2025 ) . Reproduction also takes different forms: Webster (2023) documents both image and template reproduction, and Bright Ending ( Chen et al., 2025 ) examines local memorization in which only part of an image is copied. These perspectives provide complementary accounts of what is reproduced and how memorization is represented in the model. Inference-time mitigation. Existing methods intervene at different points in generation. Random prompt perturbations disrupt the conditioning associated with reproduction ( Somepalli et al., 2023b ) , while gradient-based prompt adjustment optimizes text embeddings to reduce the magnitude of text-conditional noise predictions ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . Guidance-based methods delay or reverse classifier-free guidance to escape memorization basins ( Jain et al., 2025 ) ; Anti-Memorization Guidance combines guidance terms targeting image duplication, caption duplication, and prompt specificity ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . Initial-noise adjustment searches for starting points that permit earlier escape from memorization basins ( Han et al., 2025 ) . Bright Ending ( Chen et al., 2025 ) localizes copied regions using EOS-token attention at the final denoising step and uses the resulting spatial mask to focus detection and prompt optimization on those regions. For direct attention modification, Ren et al. (2024) combine summary-token masking with an increase in the start-of-sequence (SOS) token’s logit before softmax; the latter shifts attention toward SOS and reduces the attention weights assigned to prompt words. Our method instead redistributes attention across token positions before reinforcing content contributions, preserving the original prompt and initial noise without input optimization. Attention control for semantic fidelity. Cross-attention control also supports the expression of prompt semantics. Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) reuses attention maps to preserve spatial layout during text-based image editing. Structured Diffusion ( Feng et al., 2023 ) incorporates linguistic structure into cross-attention guidance to improve compositional generation. SynGen ( Rassin et al., 2023 ) uses syntactic relations to align the attention maps of entities and their modifiers, improving attribute binding. Attend-and-Excite ( Chefer et al., 2023 ) addresses neglected subjects by smoothing their spatial attention maps and iteratively optimizing the latent to strengthen their activations. We share the goal of making generated images more faithfully reflect prompt content. Our intervention redistributes attention along token positions and directly amplifies the resulting content contributions, coupling this semantic objective with memorization mitigation rather than optimizing a subject-specific spatial attention objective. 3 Reinforcing redistributed cross-attention We reinforce prompt content to support useful alternatives during mitigation, while controlling its allocation across token positions (Figure 1 ). We first redistribute attention, then reinforce content within the resulting pattern and selectively attenuate padding contributions. This order makes amplification act on a new mixture of token values. We formalize the operator, analyze reinforcement with localized dilution, and adapt it to DeepFloyd IF. 3.1 Redistribute, reinforce, and preserve context At sampling step k ∈ { 0 , … , T − 1 } k\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\} , cross-attention computes A k = softmax ⁡ ( Q k ​ K k ⊤ / d ) , O k = A k ​ V k . The extension bounds the effect of value variation using cumulative attention transport, identifying when the resulting mass increase compensates for this variation while attention on the original token set decreases. It therefore extends the analysis beyond components whose entire kernel neighborhood lies within content. Increasing the smoothing width can further reduce the fraction returned to the original set, but it also increases transport distance and the associated coherence requirement. Section 4.3 tests content reinforcement within our method, and Sections 4.4 and 4.5 examine the roles of allocation and guidance magnitude. 3.3 Transfer to DeepFloyd IF IF uses T5 conditioning and attention over added text keys and image keys. We apply the same operator to Stage I’s text-key block. Because T5 has no CLIP start token, smoothing spans the entire text block; content positions precede EOS, and positions after EOS receive λ p \lambda_{p} . Image keys are unchanged, and Stage II uses its original attention. The transfer uses the SD-selected configuration without IF-specific strength tuning. This adaptation tests the design with a different text encoder and pixel-space denoising while retaining the same redistribution-and-reinforcement rule. 4 Experiments We evaluate whether redistribution and reinforcement can jointly reduce training-image similarity while retaining prompt-consistent generation. After benchmarking the suppression–quality trade-off, we test whether stronger content conditioning remains useful during mitigation (Figure 4 ), whether redistribution improves the trade-off at fixed token gains (Table 1 ), and whether the effect is explained by guidance magnitude alone (Table 2 ). We then examine the EOS suppression boundary, transfer to a different model family, and selective application with an existing detector. 4.1 Evaluation setup Models and comparisons. The baseline benchmark uses 500 memorized prompts for SD v1.4 and 219 for SD v2.0 from prior work ( Webster, 2023 ; Ren et al., 2024 ) . We generate ten images per prompt with 50 steps and CFG scale 7, using DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) for v1.4 and Euler for v2.0. Baselines are random token addition (RTA; Somepalli et al., 2023b ), gradient-based prompt adjustment (GPA; Wen et al., 2024 ), cross-attention scaling (CS; Ren et al., 2024 ), opposite guidance with a dynamic transition point (DTP; Jain et al., 2025 ), and initial-noise adjustment (AIN; Han et al., 2025 ). Figure 2 includes every recorded operating point. Design and mechanism studies. Controlled studies use SD v1.4 with the same DDIM schedule and CFG scale, producing 512 × 512 512\times 512 outputs. The EOS-boundary sweep covers 500 prompts with four images each; redistribution and guidance controls use a common subset of the same benchmark. Compared settings share initial random draws. Metrics. We assess training-image similarity with SSCD ( Pizzi et al., 2022 ) , prompt alignment with CLIP cosine similarity, and learned preference with ImageReward ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . In the controlled SD studies, each generated image is compared with its prompt’s available ground-truth references using the maximum SSCD, and scores are averaged over samples. Figure 2: Mitigation–quality trade-offs on (a) SD v1.4 and (b) SD v2.0. All recorded operating points are shown; lines connect settings within each method. Lower-right is preferable. 4.2 Memorization–quality trade-offs Empirical Pareto-frontier performance. In Figure 2 , each of our four operating points lies on the empirical Pareto frontier in both the SSCD–CLIP and SSCD–ImageReward comparisons, on both models: no evaluated alternative improves one objective without worsening the other. Varying the width traverses this trade-off, with smaller widths favoring quality and larger widths favoring stronger suppression. For example, our method ( σ = 4 \sigma=4 ) and per-sample AIN (target 0.9) both report SSCD 0.2265 on SD v1.4; ours attains higher CLIP (0.2731 versus 0.2647) and ImageReward ( − 0.2374 -0.2374 versus − 0.3522 -0.3522 ). Against the attention-based CS baseline, our σ = 1 \sigma=1 setting attains lower SSCD and higher CLIP than every evaluated CS setting on both models. On SD v2.0, it also achieves higher ImageReward. Figure 3: Prompt-consistent alternatives. Comparison with GPA and CS for three prompts, with training references shown for context. Our method retains the green kitchen, fish-patterned blanket, and performance context in alternative compositions. Prompt-consistent alternatives. Figure 3 compares how mitigation methods retain prompt content. For the performance prompt, GPA shows two people posing together, while CS shows a portrait of the subject. Our output depicts the subject performing with a handheld microphone, making the requested activity more explicit than in these baseline outputs while departing from the training reference’s guitar-playing composition. The kitchen and blanket examples further illustrate alternative depictions that retain the requested green interior and fish motif. 4.3 Reinforcing redistributed content With Gaussian redistribution and padding suppression retained, λ w = 2 \lambda_{w}=2 yields higher CLIP than λ w = 1 \lambda_{w}=1 at comparable SSCD, as shown in Figure 4 . This improvement shows that stronger content conditioning can support prompt alignment without undoing the achieved suppression. Between these endpoints, SSCD responds non-monotonically: it first rises and then falls back to a comparable level at gain 2, while the wider sweep to 3 extends this decline. In the accompanying example, at λ w = 1 \lambda_{w}=1 the pillow is blue but the guitar is brown; at λ w = 2 \lambda_{w}=2 , the guitar itself is blue, matching the requested attribute. These observations support reinforcement as a means of expressing useful prompt information during mitigation, without uniformly strengthening reproduction of the training reference. This generation-level behavior complements the local compatibility result in Eq. The local analysis identifies conditions under which reinforcement preserves shared value information while redistribution dilutes localized attention, and controlled comparisons show quality recovery from redistribution at fixed token gains. Our method attains empirical Pareto-frontier performance on two Stable Diffusion benchmarks. An SD-selected configuration also reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning. The resulting principle is to reinforce useful prompt content during mitigation, using redistribution to improve the balance between reproduction suppression and prompt-consistent generation.
